Hong-Hoa (Emma) Hoang

Houston, Texas, USA

I'm an application scientist and cell biologist with 10+ years in industry and academic labs. I work on label-free live-cell and organoid imaging, cell-based assay development, 3D microfluidic models and preclinical in vivo pharmacology.

From 2021 to 2026 I was on the Bio-Imaging Team at Tomocube Inc. in Daejeon, South Korea, a company that builds label-free 3D microscopes and AI image-analysis software. My job was to turn customers' research questions into imaging workflows that work: I ran demonstrations on their samples, wrote application notes and SOPs, and tested new microscopes and software before release. In my last two years I led a set of smaller studies for the company's biggest project, a new microscope for imaging whole organoids.

Before that, I ran rodent drug studies at NeuMed Inc. and built PDMS microfluidic tumor and gut models at Sungkyunkwan University, which led to four papers, including one in PNAS. I have an M.S. in Bionanotechnology from Ewha Womans University and a B.S. in Biochemistry from the University of Science, VNU-HCM.

I'm looking for Application Scientist and Field Application Scientist roles in cell imaging, life-science instruments or cell-based assays. I speak English, Korean and Vietnamese.

how I work

I own my workWhen a project is mine, I see it through. I owned a prototype test plan, took a microfluidic application from the first chip test to an application note and four conference posters, and kept the team's cell lab running.
I find the root causeI would rather know why something fails than work around it. I traced cell death in long runs to humidity loss in the chamber, and autofocus failures at a customer site to a warped chamber frame.
I lead small projects that move big onesFor a new organoid microscope, I planned and led focused studies (near-infrared wavelengths, fluorescence uniformity, a 4-color dye panel, AI training data), each answering one question for the hardware, software and AI teams.

Deep 3D imaging of intact organoids

Organoid & 3D imaging applications · Tomocube

Challenge
Thick 3D samples lose image quality with depth, and labels limit how long one sample can be followed.
Approach
Optimized sample prep, imaging settings and fluorescence staining for human and mouse organoids (intestine, liver, lung), normal and tumor. I led the smaller studies behind it: a near-infrared wavelength comparison (850/890/940 nm), fluorescence uniformity tests and a 4-color fixed panel.
Result
A shared SOP for imaging up to ~500 µm deep, with a 4-color fixed panel to confirm structures.
~500 µmimaging depth
120 hlongest time-lapse
3organ types
For your team  I can take a new sample type from first culture to an imaging protocol customers can follow.
← all projects

Turning image quality into numbers biologists trust

AI image-analysis validation · Tomocube

With the AI engineers, I built the ground-truth datasets and defined the scoring (F1, IoU) that decide whether a segmentation model is good enough for real measurements.

Paired label-free + fluorescence images
→
Ground-truth nucleus masks
→
Model inference
→
Object-level F1 at IoU
→
Review false positives / negatives
ScoreWhat it looks likeWhat it means for the biology
False negativea nucleus the model missedcell counts and growth are underestimated
False positiveone nucleus split in two, or debriscounts and density are overestimated
Low IoUmask edges off the true boundarysize and shape measurements drift
High F1 at IoUmost nuclei found, accurate edgescounts and sizes can be trusted

Tools: napari, CellProfiler, Cellpose, StarDist, ilastik, ImageJ/Fiji and TomoAnalysis.

For your team  I use the same checks on any analysis software before customers rely on its numbers.

Long live-cell runs and instrument validation

Live-cell assays & instrument validation · Tomocube

  1. Long, stable runs

    Live-cell time-lapse up to 120 h, including H₂O₂ stress and recovery under flow in microfluidic chips; presented at 4 international conferences.

  2. Validation & fault finding

    Tested new microscopes and software before release and owned the test plan for a prototype. When cells kept dying in long runs, I worked through the chamber piece by piece (humidifier, leaks, evaporation) and validated a fix. I traced autofocus failures at a customer site to a warped chamber frame.

  3. Customer delivery

    10+ end-to-end imaging studies and ~10 demonstrations on customers' own samples, from pilot dose-finding to a full 96-well study.

For your team  I know where long live-cell runs fail, and how to explain the fix to a customer.

Microfluidic tumor & tissue models

Researcher, Microfluidic Cell Culture · Sungkyunkwan University · 2015–2017

I designed chips in AutoCAD and fabricated them in PDMS to grow cells in 3D under gravity- and pump-driven perfusion. Each device recreated a part of the tumor or tissue environment that flat culture can't.
